cases.holding: The court held that at an adjudicatory hearing the circuit court must focus solely on whether the child was neglected rather than apportion blame among parents, and, finding the State had failed to prove neglect as to Arthur Jr., reversed the circuit court and dismissed the amended wardship petition.
cases.quote: It is the burden of the State to prove allegations of neglect by a preponderance of the evidence.

relevance.DEC-05: Sets the burden and the sole question the circuit court may decide when the agency files a wardship petition in Illinois.
relevance.INP-07: The neglect allegations rested on medical-neglect findings reported by a DCFS investigator after a health-care contact, and the court held that evidence insufficient.
relevance.INP-12: The children were taken into emergency temporary custody before the petition was filed, and the court measured that action against the statutory proof standard.
relevance.OUT-05: Because the State did not carry the preponderance burden, the correct disposition was dismissal of the petition.

cases.holding: The court affirmed the appellate court's reversal of a neglect adjudication, holding that a mother who left her children with a boyfriend she had no reason to suspect, and who took the injured child straight to hospital, did not place them in an injurious environment.
cases.quote: If the State fails to prove the allegations of abuse, neglect, or dependence by a preponderance of the evidence, the court must dismiss the petition.

relevance.DEC-01: Confirms that where proof falls short of a preponderance the correct outcome is no finding and no case.
relevance.DEC-06: The trial court found the parents fit and closed the case, illustrating the no-petition/service-only path the statute contemplates.
relevance.INP-07: The neglect finding rested in part on Pediatric Resource Center medical records generated after a hospital presentation.
relevance.OUT-05: States the mandatory dismissal rule that governs case closure for unproven allegations.

cases.holding: The court held that 'sound discretion' is not a standard of proof and that the State must prove by a preponderance of the evidence at the best-interests stage that termination of parental rights is in the child's best interest, remanding for a new best-interests hearing.
cases.quote: at a best-interests hearing, the parent's interest in maintaining the parent-child relationship must yield to the child's interest in a stable, loving home life

relevance.OUT-02: Fixes the two-step Illinois termination structure: clear and convincing evidence of unfitness, then preponderance at the best-interests stage.

cases.holding: The court reinstated the abuse and neglect findings and the dispositional order, reaffirming that the adjudicatory hearing asks only whether the child was abused or neglected, and remanded for proof that the Indian Child Welfare Act's notice requirements had been satisfied.
cases.quote: We agree with the GAL that this case must be remanded for proof of compliance with the Indian Child Welfare Act.

relevance.ACT-03: Foster placement of the siblings could not stand without record proof that ICWA notice obligations had been discharged.
relevance.DEC-04: Bare notification to the Bureau of Indian Affairs before removal is not enough; the record must show what followed.
relevance.INP-11: The leading Illinois Supreme Court statement that unresolved Indian-ancestry information triggers ICWA compliance before a case can proceed.
relevance.OUT-06: The case began with the earlier death of an infant sibling, and the court treated that history as bearing on the siblings' environment.

cases.holding: The court reversed the appellate court and affirmed the termination judgment, holding that the three recognized per se conflict situations are a closed set and that counsel's earlier brief service as guardian ad litem for the child did not create a per se conflict.
cases.quote: That is a closed set, and any other situations may be examined for an actual conflict of interest.

relevance.FAIL-01: Narrows the circumstances in which a reviewing court will reverse a termination judgment for conflicted counsel.
relevance.OUT-02: Governs ineffective-assistance and conflict-of-interest challenges to Illinois termination-of-parental-rights judgments.

cases.holding: The court held that the State's failure to file the separate notice specifying the nine-month period relied on for the reasonable-progress unfitness ground was a forfeitable pleading defect, and reinstated the circuit court's unfitness finding.
cases.quote: the State's failure to file a separate notice pleading identifying the nine-month period or periods at issue constitutes a pleading defect

relevance.ACT-02: The reasonable-progress ground measures a parent's performance against the court-ordered service plan during defined nine-month windows.
relevance.FAIL-01: Explains when a pleading irregularity in the State's case will and will not support reversal on appeal.

cases.case_name: Lyon v. Department of Children & Family Services
cases.holding: The court held that DCFS violated Lyon's due process rights by combining the low credible-evidence standard for indicating a report and deciding the first-stage appeal with delays beyond its own regulatory deadlines, and affirmed expungement from the State Central Register.
cases.quote: we require strict statutory and regulatory compliance only if the Department uses the credible-evidence standard to indicate a report and to consider a first-stage appeal

relevance.DEC-01: Describes the credible-evidence screening threshold DCFS applies when deciding whether a report is indicated or unfounded.
relevance.DEC-03: The controlling Illinois authority on the process due before a substantiated (indicated) finding may stand on the central register.
relevance.INP-01: Mandated-reporter allegations against a school employee drove the register listing at issue.
relevance.INP-02: Applies to any report, however originated, that DCFS indicates against a named subject.
relevance.INP-06: The hotline-to-register pipeline is precisely the system whose standard of proof and timeliness the court measured.
relevance.INP-10: Governs the escalation from screening to a completed investigation with a register entry.
relevance.FAIL-01: A court will set aside an indicated finding when DCFS misses the deadlines its own rules impose.

cases.holding: The court held that a conviction under a facially unconstitutional statute is void ab initio and cannot be used to establish depravity, affirming the appellate court's reversal of the unfitness finding and remanding for DCFS to attempt proof on other grounds.
cases.quote: Today, we hold simply that he cannot be found depraved and therefore unfit under section 1(D)(i) of the Adoption Act based on his legally nonexistent and now-vacated 2008 AUUW conviction.

relevance.OUT-02: Limits the criminal-conviction route to parental unfitness and restates that the parental liberty interest survives imperfect parenting.

cases.holding: The court held that the circuit court could not disregard a DCFS administrative abuse finding by conducting its own de novo review, reversed the change of custody as against the manifest weight of the evidence, and reinstated DCFS as guardian with power to consent to adoption.
cases.quote: The court, without authority, rejected an administrative finding that the Wards abused Austin after conducting a de novo review of the matter.

relevance.ACT-03: Defines the respective roles of the juvenile court and DCFS as guardian over a child's foster placement.
relevance.ACT-04: The custody dispute was over placing the child with the family that had been indicated for abusing him, rather than his existing caregiver.
relevance.ACT-06: DCFS as guardian was the entity contacted by the hospital to consent to the injured child's medical treatment.
relevance.DEC-03: An indicated administrative finding retains probative force in later juvenile-court proceedings and cannot simply be ignored.
relevance.INP-04: Illustrates a guardian ad litem motion in juvenile court triggering renewed agency and judicial scrutiny of a placement.
relevance.FAIL-01: Shows the limits on a circuit court's power to reverse an agency's abuse finding.

cases.holding: The court held that standing for a guardianship petition under the Probate Act is governed by section 11-5(b) and that a fit parent who is willing and able to make day-to-day child-care decisions is entitled to custody, remanding for application of that standard.
cases.quote: if respondent is a fit person who is competent to transact his own business, he is entitled to custody of R.L.S.

relevance.OUT-03: Controls when a non-parent may obtain guardianship of a minor over a surviving parent's objection in Illinois.

cases.case_name: Doe-3 v. McLean County Unit District No. 5 Board of Directors
cases.holding: The court held school officials owed no affirmative common-law duty to warn or report, but that plaintiffs stated a willful and wanton claim based on defendants' alleged misrepresentation of a teacher's record to a subsequent employer, and remanded for further proceedings.
cases.quote: the common law does not recognize an affirmative duty to act for the protection of another in the absence of a special relationship between the parties

relevance.INP-01: Establishes that in Illinois the reporting duty of school personnel is statutory under ANCRA, not a freestanding common-law duty.
relevance.INP-02: Confirms that the absence of a special relationship defeats a common-law duty claim against a non-reporter.
relevance.INP-08: The leading Illinois authority on educator responsibility when school staff learn of suspected abuse by a colleague.

cases.case_name: Harris v. One Hope United, Inc.
cases.holding: The court declined to recognize a self-critical analysis privilege in Illinois and affirmed the order compelling a DCFS contractor to produce its internal priority review report on an infant's death during intact family services.
cases.quote: the type of information sought in discovery here is not subject to a "self-critical analysis privilege" that would protect it from disclosure

relevance.FAIL-04: Internal agency reviews of a child's death while under supervision are discoverable in the ensuing wrongful-death action.
relevance.FAIL-06: Rejects a privilege that would have let a child-welfare provider withhold its own post-fatality review.
relevance.INP-09: Post-fatality priority review reports are an oversight product, and this case fixes their discoverability.
relevance.OUT-06: Arose directly from a fatality of a child whose family was receiving agency intact-family services.
relevance.PMC-02: Supports access to the internal audit and review records that accountability work depends on.
relevance.PMC-04: Confirms that fatality-review material is not shielded from litigants by a common-law privilege.
relevance.PMC-05: Illinois' highest court leaves any new confidentiality privilege to the legislature, favoring disclosure in its absence.

cases.holding: The court affirmed the neglect and unfitness findings and reversed the appellate court's Fifth Amendment ruling, holding that on this record the father failed to prove the court-ordered sex-offender counseling requirement compelled him to incriminate himself.
cases.quote: the record in this case fails to support the appellate court's conclusion that the circuit court's order had the effect of requiring Eugene to incriminate himself

relevance.ACT-02: Defines the constitutional limits on what a juvenile court may require of a parent in a court-ordered service plan.
relevance.INP-04: Prior DCFS indicated reports and an earlier juvenile adjudication were carried forward by collateral estoppel into the new proceeding.

cases.holding: The court reversed the appellate court and reinstated the neglect adjudication, holding that the circuit court properly considered all eight incidents of the father's violent and erratic conduct, not only those occurring in the children's presence.
cases.quote: An adjudication of neglect is to be reviewed based on the totality of the evidence.

relevance.DEC-02: Supports accepting and investigating a report on an accumulated pattern of conduct rather than a single incident.
relevance.DEC-05: Establishes the evidentiary frame for an injurious-environment petition built on a course of parental conduct.

cases.holding: The court held that the State's reliance on a computerized name search while ignoring other leads was not the diligent inquiry section 2-16(2) requires, so service by publication failed to confer personal jurisdiction and the default termination judgment was void.
cases.quote: Section 2-16(2) unequivocally requires a diligent inquiry in every instance when service by publication is used, regardless of whether that inquiry ultimately proves successful in locating the parent.

relevance.DEC-05: Sets the notice prerequisites the State must satisfy when it opens a dependency case against an absent parent.
relevance.FAIL-01: A default termination entered on defective publication service is void and must be vacated.
relevance.OUT-02: Termination judgments obtained without a genuine diligent search for the parent cannot stand.

cases.holding: The court affirmed reversal of a termination order, holding that habitual drunkenness under section 1(D)(k) requires clear and convincing proof of a fixed habit during the one-year period immediately preceding the petition, which the State had not supplied.
cases.quote: the State must, at a minimum, present clear and convincing evidence of habitual drunkenness during the critical one-year period immediately preceding the filing of its termination petition

relevance.ACT-01: Substance-use treatment ordered or offered to a parent cannot be converted into an unfitness finding without proof tied to the statutory window.
relevance.OUT-02: Controls the substance-abuse ground for parental unfitness in Illinois and its temporal limits.

cases.holding: The court affirmed reversal of the unfitness finding as to a child born during the nine-month reasonable-progress period, holding the statute's literal language, not convenience, controls which children a reasonable-progress finding can reach.
cases.quote: when conducting such proceedings, it is not simple logic, but the literal language of the statute that must control

relevance.ACT-02: The reasonable-progress ground is measured child by child against the statutory period, not extrapolated across a sibling group.
relevance.INP-03: The case entered the system through a Peoria police response to a domestic dispute that generated a hotline call to DCFS.
relevance.OUT-05: A termination petition that overreaches the statute's literal terms must fail as to the child not covered.

cases.holding: The court held that a parent's appeal challenging only the neglect finding was moot where the unchallenged dependency finding independently supported the adjudication, and affirmed the judgments below.
cases.quote: We find that D.H.E.'s appeal, challenging only the circuit court's neglect finding and failing to challenge the dependency finding, is moot.

relevance.FAIL-01: Limits the circumstances in which an appellate court will disturb an adjudicatory finding a parent disputes.
relevance.OUT-05: Explains when an unchallenged alternative ground makes review of an adjudication unnecessary.

cases.holding: The court held the statutory provision making permanency orders immediately appealable as of right violated separation of powers and severed it, but held such orders may be reviewed by discretionary petition under Rule 306(a)(5), remanding for the appellate court to decide whether to take the appeal.
cases.quote: we conclude that the appellate review provided by Rule 306(a)(5) maintains the best balance between protecting parental rights and ensuring expeditious resolution of the child's placement status

relevance.OUT-01: Determines how a parent may seek review when the permanency goal moves away from return home.
relevance.OUT-05: Sets the appellate route for interim orders short of a final order closing the case.

cases.holding: The court affirmed dismissal of the State's appeal, holding that an order denying a petition to terminate parental rights is not final and appealable because the Act permits successive termination petitions.
cases.quote: the October 5, 2001, order is not final because it did not end the litigation of the parties on the issue of termination of parental rights

relevance.OUT-01: A denial of termination leaves the case open and reunification efforts continuing rather than concluding the litigation.
relevance.OUT-05: Distinguishes a denial of relief from a final closing order for purposes of appellate jurisdiction.

cases.holding: The court affirmed the order directing the county to pay appointed appellate counsel for an indigent mother whose parental rights were terminated in an adoption proceeding that grew out of a juvenile abuse and neglect case.
cases.quote: the result in this case is mandated by the Illinois and United States Constitutions and by long-standing judicial interpretation of the Juvenile Court Act

relevance.FAIL-01: Appointment of counsel on appeal was the mechanism by which the mother obtained reversal of a proceeding conducted without a lawyer.
relevance.OUT-03: Adoption-based permanency proceedings that follow a juvenile case carry the juvenile case's procedural safeguards, including counsel.

cases.holding: The court affirmed a circuit court order directing DCFS to remove and reassign a caseworker team that had failed its statutory reporting duty, holding the order neither exceeded the Juvenile Court Act nor violated separation of powers.
cases.quote: The ultimate determination of which caseworkers to assign to the matter, therefore, remained within the discretion of DCFS.

relevance.ACT-02: Marks how far a juvenile court may go in policing agency performance of court-ordered casework.
relevance.INP-01: The order was premised on the assigned caseworkers' failure to satisfy their statutory duty to report to the court.
relevance.INP-04: Illustrates judicial direction to the agency mid-case as a trigger for renewed agency action.

cases.case_name: Burris v. Department of Children & Family Services
cases.holding: The court reversed, holding that once a court has entered a judicial finding of child neglect on the same issue, section 7.16 of the Reporting Act and DCFS Rule 336.190(a)(3) require dismissal of an administrative appeal seeking expungement of the indicated report.
cases.quote: plaintiff's administrative appeal requesting expungement of the report of child neglect should have been dismissed pursuant to section 7.16 of the Reporting Act

relevance.DEC-03: A juvenile-court neglect finding forecloses the parallel administrative route for contesting the indicated register entry.
relevance.INP-06: The indicated finding traced back to a DCFS hotline call, and this case governs how far the subject may contest it.
relevance.FAIL-01: Defines when a reviewing court will and will not reopen an agency's substantiated finding.

cases.holding: The court reversed a dispositional order placing an Indian child in foster care entered without qualified expert witness testimony, holding ICWA section 1912(e) must be satisfied before any foster care placement, and remanded for an ICWA-compliant dispositional hearing.
cases.quote: ICWA rules for foster care placement applied at the time that A.M., a child of Indigenous standing, was removed from her father's home

relevance.ACT-03: No foster care placement of an Indian child may be ordered without the ICWA qualified expert witness showing.
relevance.ACT-05: The dispute arose around an order of protection restricting the parents' contact pending the ICWA-defective disposition.
relevance.INP-11: The most recent published Illinois application of ICWA's qualified expert witness and active efforts requirements.

cases.holding: The court reversed an order closing the case to private guardianship with the paternal grandmother, holding the best-interests finding was against the manifest weight of the evidence where the mother had complied with services and every caseworker recommended return home.
cases.quote: The circuit court's finding that this was in K.W.'s best interest was against the manifest weight of the evidence.

relevance.ACT-01: The mother's full engagement in recommended services was central to the court's rejection of a permanency change.
relevance.ACT-04: Addresses when placement with a relative should be converted into permanent private guardianship instead of return home.
relevance.FAIL-01: A recent reversal of a permanency decision that ran against the agency's own recommendations.
relevance.INP-05: The mother's voluntary compliance and self-initiated treatment were treated as weighing toward reunification.
relevance.OUT-01: Reaffirms that reunification remains the goal where the parent has corrected the conditions and the bond is intact.
relevance.OUT-03: Guardianship is not a substitute for return home absent evidence that reunification efforts have failed.

cases.case_name: Hernandez ex rel. Hernandez v. Foster
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
cases.holding: The court affirmed qualified immunity on the initial removal of an Illinois child but vacated as to continuing to hold him after probable cause dissipated and as to the coerced safety plan, remanding those claims for further proceedings.
cases.quote: Probable cause is determined on the basis of the facts and circumstances known to the defendants at the time of the conduct in issue

relevance.ACT-01: Treats a DCFS safety plan as an option parents may accept, while coercion into one can itself deprive them of liberty.
relevance.ACT-05: Safety-plan restrictions on parental contact are analyzed as deprivations of liberty triggering a right to a hearing.
relevance.DEC-04: The governing Seventh Circuit rule for judging an Illinois DCFS decision to take a child into protective custody.
relevance.DEC-06: The leading analysis of DCFS safety plans used in place of immediate removal.
relevance.INP-03: The investigation began after hospital staff notified DCFS of a suspicious fracture.
relevance.INP-12: Holds that the Juvenile Court Act's 48-hour window does not license continued custody once probable cause has dissipated.
relevance.FAIL-02: The controlling Illinois-specific authority on section 1983 liability for removal and continued withholding of a child.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
cases.holding: The court reversed dismissal of a former foster child's section 1983 claims, holding that a child removed from his home on allegedly fabricated neglect allegations stated Fourth Amendment and substantive due process claims that survived the defendants' immunity defenses in part.
cases.quote: a seizure is reasonable if it is pursuant to a court order, if it is supported by probable cause, or if it is justified by exigent circumstances

relevance.DEC-04: States the three—and only three—justifications for removing a child from the home without violating the Fourth Amendment.
relevance.INP-03: The removal followed a coordinated law-enforcement and agency response to relatives' neglect allegations in Mercer County, Illinois.
relevance.INP-12: Defines the constitutional ceiling on emergency protective custody in Illinois.
relevance.OUT-04: The plaintiff sued only after reaching eighteen, illustrating that claims arising from foster care may be pursued on aging out.
relevance.FAIL-02: The foundational Seventh Circuit decision on unlawful removal of an Illinois child under section 1983.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
cases.holding: The court largely upheld injunctive relief requiring DCFS to weigh exculpatory evidence under the credible-evidence standard and to give child-care workers a pre-deprivation conference and expedited appeal, while holding foster parents lack a protected liberty or property interest.
cases.quote: It also requires that the investigator take into account all of the available evidence that tends to show that abuse or neglect did or did not occur.

relevance.ACT-04: Holds that foster parents have no protected liberty or property interest in their license or foster care payments.
relevance.DEC-01: Defines what an investigator must consider before a report is screened as indicated rather than unfounded.
relevance.DEC-02: Describes the DCFS investigative scheme and the minimum quality of fact-finding due process demands of it.
relevance.DEC-03: The controlling federal decision on the process due before DCFS enters and discloses an indicated finding.
relevance.DEC-06: Explains DCFS safety plans as a less extreme alternative to removal, offered without a prior hearing.
relevance.INP-01: Mandated-reporter allegations feed the register system whose accuracy safeguards this case imposed.
relevance.INP-02: Applies to every report DCFS indicates, regardless of who made it.
relevance.INP-06: Describes the DCFS hotline and investigation pipeline the injunction reformed.
relevance.INP-09: A structural federal injunction remains a principal oversight lever over Illinois child-protection investigations.
relevance.INP-10: Governs the escalation from an intake report to a recorded, disclosable indicated finding.
relevance.FAIL-03: Class-wide federal litigation is the practical enforcement mechanism for systemic Illinois investigative failures.
relevance.PMC-01: Court supervision of DCFS practice supplements federal performance monitoring of the state's child-welfare system.
relevance.PMC-02: The district court's detailed findings function as an audit of DCFS investigative practice.
relevance.PMC-03: Judicial review of DCFS procedures substitutes here for the independent citizen-panel review CAPTA contemplates.
relevance.PMC-06: A worked example of systemic pattern analysis of agency decision-making driving structural reform.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
cases.holding: The court affirmed denial of qualified immunity, holding that a caseworker's under-the-clothes examination of children at a private school exceeded the principal's consent to interview them and violated their clearly established Fourth Amendment rights.
cases.quote: the searches of the children's bodies to investigate child abuse were presumptively unreasonable, unless they fall within an exception to the warrant requirement of the Fourth Amendment

relevance.DEC-02: Sets the Fourth Amendment limits on how far an accepted investigation may go without a warrant or valid consent.
relevance.INP-08: Governs child-protection interviews and examinations conducted on private school premises in this circuit.
relevance.FAIL-02: Bodily searches of children during an investigation, without consent or a warrant, expose caseworkers to section 1983 liability.

cases.case_name: K.H. ex rel. Murphy v. Morgan
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that an Illinois foster child has a clearly established right not to be handed to a caretaker the state's caseworkers know or suspect is likely to abuse or neglect her, while rejecting any right to a stable foster-home environment, and affirmed denial of qualified immunity in part.
cases.quote: a prima facie right not to be placed with a foster parent who the state's caseworkers and supervisors know or suspect is likely to abuse or neglect the foster child

relevance.ACT-03: The constitutional floor DCFS must meet when it selects and approves a foster placement in Illinois.
relevance.ACT-04: The court distinguishes placement with a relative from placement in a licensed foster home for duty purposes.
relevance.OUT-04: The state's duty runs for as long as the child remains in its custody, including through repeated moves.
relevance.OUT-06: Establishes agency liability where a child in state custody suffers serious harm at a known-dangerous placement.
relevance.FAIL-04: The governing Illinois authority on constitutional responsibility for harm to a child under agency supervision.
relevance.PMC-04: Frames the constitutional duty whose breach fatality and serious-injury reviews are meant to detect.

cases.case_name: Doyle v. Camelot Care Centers, Inc.
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that the credible-evidence standard combined with a belated post-deprivation hearing denied child-care workers adequate process when DCFS disclosed indicated findings to their employers, though the individual DCFS defendants were immune and the private employers were not state actors.
cases.quote: we conclude that the credible evidence standard, operating in conjunction with a belated post-deprivation hearing, failed to afford adequate process to Ms. Doyle and Mr. Konold

relevance.DEC-03: Identifies the occupational liberty interest at stake when DCFS indicates and discloses a finding against a child-care worker.
relevance.INP-10: The disclosure of an escalated investigation's outcome to employers is what triggered the constitutional injury.
relevance.FAIL-03: Federal courts enforce due process limits that Illinois' own register procedures repeatedly failed to satisfy.
relevance.FAIL-05: Recognizes agency blacklisting from a profession as an actionable deprivation rather than mere reputational harm.
relevance.PMC-01: Judicial findings of systemic register-process failure supply an external performance check on the state agency.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that non-parties, including the Cook County Public Guardian, had no right to intervene in or attend in-chambers status conferences implementing the B.H. consent decree governing the Illinois DCFS, and that the public had no First Amendment right of access to those conferences.
cases.quote: we hold that non-parties have no right to be present at these in-chambers conferences

relevance.INP-09: The B.H. consent decree is the long-running structural oversight regime over the Illinois child-welfare system.
relevance.FAIL-03: A federal consent decree is the operative remedy for systemic Illinois child-welfare performance failures.
relevance.FAIL-06: Marks the limits of public access to the implementation of a child-welfare reform decree.
relevance.PMC-01: Court-supervised monitoring under the decree parallels and predates federal CFSR performance review of Illinois.
relevance.PMC-02: Monitor reports and the agency's responses under the decree are the principal public audit record of DCFS.
relevance.PMC-03: Decree monitoring largely occupies the independent-review function citizen panels are meant to serve in Illinois.
relevance.PMC-05: Defines what decree-implementation material is publicly accessible and what remains in chambers.
relevance.PMC-06: Illustrates how systemic monitoring data about a state agency is generated, published, and bounded.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
cases.holding: The court affirmed summary judgment for the caseworker defendants, holding the parents had not shown racial animus and that their equal protection and section 1985(3) conspiracy claims arising from a disabled child's removal therefore failed.
cases.quote: To establish "purpose" under prong two, a plaintiff must demonstrate racial, ethnic, or other class-based "invidiously discriminatory animus behind the conspirators' actions."

relevance.INP-08: The investigation began with a referral from school personnel who observed the child's condition.
relevance.FAIL-05: States the showing a family must make to convert a removal into an actionable discrimination or retaliation claim in this circuit.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that due process requires a state to support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence before terminating parental rights, and reversed New York's use of a fair-preponderance standard.
cases.quote: due process requires that the State support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence

relevance.OUT-02: The federal constitutional floor for the unfitness stage of Illinois termination proceedings, which the legislature codified in 1983.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that Illinois violated due process and equal protection by declaring the children of an unwed father dependent without any hearing on his fitness, and reversed the Illinois Supreme Court.
cases.quote: We have concluded that all Illinois parents are constitutionally entitled to a hearing on their fitness before their children are removed from their custody.

relevance.DEC-05: An Illinois case: the State cannot obtain wardship of a child without giving each parent a fitness hearing.
relevance.INP-12: Emergency custody cannot ripen into a change of custody without the hearing due process requires.
relevance.FAIL-02: Removal without any hearing on parental fitness is itself the constitutional violation the Court identified in Illinois practice.
relevance.FAIL-05: Struck an Illinois classification that singled out unwed fathers for worse treatment than all other parents.

cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that the Due Process Clause imposed no affirmative constitutional duty on county social workers to protect a child from his father's violence while he remained in his father's custody, and affirmed judgment for the county.
cases.quote: nothing in the language of the Due Process Clause itself requires the State to protect the life, liberty, and property of its citizens against invasion by private actors

relevance.FAIL-04: The controlling federal rule that agency inaction toward a child left in the home is not, without more, a constitutional violation.
relevance.OUT-06: Establishes the limits of constitutional liability when a child suffers catastrophic injury while known to the agency.
relevance.PMC-04: Explains why fatality review and legislative reform, rather than constitutional tort, are the main accountability routes for children harmed at home.

cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Services of Durham County
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that due process does not require appointed counsel in every parental termination proceeding and left the decision to the trial court case by case, affirming the refusal to appoint counsel on this record.
cases.quote: neither can we say that the Constitution requires the appointment of counsel in every parental termination proceeding

relevance.OUT-02: The federal constitutional baseline for counsel at termination, which Illinois exceeds by statute under the Juvenile Court Act.

cases.holding: The court held that the State must prove neglect by a preponderance of the evidence and, finding that two isolated displays of a mother's temper directed at no one in the household did not establish an injurious environment, reversed the appellate and circuit courts and ordered the neglect petitions dismissed.
cases.quote: The State bears the burden of proving neglect, dependence or abuse by a preponderance of the evidence, meaning proof that makes the condition more probable than not.

relevance.DEC-01: The origin of the Illinois rule that an allegation the State cannot prove produces no finding at all, which In re Arthur H. and In re A.P. only restate.
relevance.DEC-05: The Illinois Supreme Court's original statement of the burden the State assumes the moment it files a wardship petition alleging neglect.
relevance.OUT-05: Having found the proof insufficient, the court ordered the petitions dismissed outright rather than remanding for further proceedings.

cases.holding: The court affirmed the neglect adjudication and wardship of a newborn, holding Illinois had jurisdiction under the UCCJEA even though the child was delivered in Indiana, that the ex parte shelter-care notice complaint was moot, and that the injurious-environment finding was not against the manifest weight of the evidence.
cases.quote: On review, a trial court's ruling of neglect will not be reversed unless it is against the manifest weight of the evidence.

relevance.DEC-05: Confirms that a wardship petition may be filed and sustained in Illinois for a child delivered out of state where the family's connections and the evidence are here.
relevance.OUT-05: The mirror image of the dismissal rule: an adjudication the record supports will stand rather than be closed out.
relevance.FAIL-01: Supplies the manifest-weight standard of review that governs every appellate challenge to an Illinois neglect adjudication.
relevance.INP-07: The case arose from the mother's flight from Illinois against her obstetrician's instructions and the out-of-state hospital delivery that followed.

cases.holding: The court affirmed the vacatur of a mother's admission of unfitness, holding that due process requires the circuit court to determine that a factual basis exists before accepting such an admission, and remanded for a new fitness hearing.
cases.quote: Before a circuit court can adjudicate a parent unfit and terminate parental rights, the State must prove by clear and convincing evidence that the parent is unfit.

relevance.OUT-02: The Illinois bridge between Santosky and the two-step termination structure: clear and convincing proof of unfitness comes first, best interests second.
relevance.FAIL-01: A termination judgment was undone because the circuit court took an admission of unfitness without finding a factual basis for it.

cases.holding: The court affirmed the appellate court, holding that section 1(D)(f) of the Adoption Act violates due process because it rests unfitness on prior abuse findings made by a preponderance, and remanded for a new termination hearing under the clear and convincing standard.
cases.quote: we order a new hearing on the State's petition to be conducted under the constitutionally proper standard, i.e., clear and convincing evidence

relevance.OUT-02: The Illinois Supreme Court's own application of Santosky, striking an unfitness ground that borrowed preponderance-level abuse findings from the juvenile case.
relevance.FAIL-01: Fixes the remedy when a termination was decided under the wrong standard of proof: a new hearing, not appellate reweighing of the evidence.

cases.holding: The court reversed the appellate court and reinstated both parents' unfitness findings, holding that the benchmark for reasonable progress under section 1(D)(m) takes in compliance with DCFS service plans and court directives measured against both the conditions that caused removal and conditions later discovered.
cases.quote: compliance with DCFS service plans is intimately tied to a parent's progress toward the return of the child

relevance.ACT-02: The leading Illinois decision on how compliance with a court-ordered DCFS service plan figures in the reasonable-progress ground for unfitness.
relevance.ACT-01: Holds that a service plan must reasonably relate to remedying conditions that could give rise to a finding of abuse or neglect, not to administrative directives unrelated to return of the child.
relevance.OUT-02: Supplies the substantive content of the section 1(D)(m) unfitness ground that In re S.L. and In re D.C. address only procedurally.

cases.holding: The court held that section 1(D)(q) of the Adoption Act, which made a conviction for attempted murder or aggravated battery of a child conclusive proof of unfitness, denies equal protection because section 1(D)(i) lets parents convicted of comparable offenses rebut the presumption.
cases.quote: Therefore, we hold section 1(D)(q) unconstitutional as violative of equal protection.

relevance.OUT-02: Supplies the depravity framework and its rebuttable presumption that In re N.G. later limits, and holds that a conviction-based unfitness ground must leave room for rebuttal.
relevance.FAIL-05: Struck a statutory classification that withheld from one group of parents the rebuttal rights given to others convicted of the same offenses.

cases.holding: The court affirmed the unfitness finding, holding that section 1(D)(m)'s nine-month evaluation period applies to both the reasonable-efforts and the reasonable-progress grounds and runs from the adjudication of neglect, abuse or dependency rather than from the dispositional order.
cases.quote: A stated purpose of the Juvenile Court Act is to secure permanency for minors who have been removed from the custody of their parents "at the earliest opportunity."

relevance.ACT-02: Fixes the nine-month window in which a parent's efforts to correct the removal conditions and progress toward return are measured against court-ordered services.
relevance.OUT-01: States the statutory expedition and permanency policy against which reunification efforts and reasonable-efforts findings are timed in Illinois.
relevance.OUT-02: Controls which period of a parent's conduct a court may consider on the section 1(D)(m) unfitness ground.

cases.holding: The court affirmed dismissal of a failure-to-warn claim, holding that Illinois adheres to the rule that absent one of the four recognized special relationships a private person owes no affirmative duty to warn or protect another from a third party's criminal conduct.
cases.quote: a private person has no duty to act affirmatively to protect another from criminal attack by a third person absent a "special relationship" between the parties

relevance.INP-01: The affirmative-duty framework Doe-3 applies to school staff: because the common law imposes no duty to warn, a reporting obligation in Illinois must come from ANCRA.
relevance.INP-02: Confirms that someone who learns of a danger to a child owes no common-law duty to act unless one of the four recognized special relationships exists.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that caseworkers who searched a private religious school and seized a student for a child-abuse interview without a warrant, court order, probable cause, consent or exigent circumstances violated the Fourth Amendment and the family's right to familial relations, but affirmed qualified immunity because those rights were not yet clearly established.
cases.quote: although child welfare caseworkers may investigate allegations of child abuse without violating parents' constitutional right to familial relations, they may not do so arbitrarily

relevance.INP-08: The foundational Seventh Circuit decision on child-abuse investigations conducted on private school premises without parental notice or consent.
relevance.DEC-02: Sets the constitutional ceiling on an accepted investigation: caseworkers may investigate, but not arbitrarily and not by warrantless entry onto private property.
relevance.FAIL-02: Holds that seizing a child at school and threatening removal without articulable evidence of abuse are constitutional violations, the analysis Michael C. v. Gresbach later applies.

cases.case_name: Siliven v. Indiana Department of Child Services
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
cases.holding: The court affirmed judgment for the caseworkers, holding that a removal made without a court order is reasonable only if supported by probable cause or exigent circumstances and that a physician's opinion of inflicted injury plus a prior abuse allegation supplied probable cause here.
cases.quote: The pertinent inquiry, then, is whether defendants had probable cause to believe that C.S.'s physical health would be seriously endangered if he was not immediately removed from his father's custody.

relevance.DEC-04: The Seventh Circuit rule Hernandez v. Foster applies: without a court order, an emergency removal stands only on probable cause or exigent circumstances.
relevance.INP-12: Supplies the objective probable-cause framework for protective custody, judged on the facts known to the caseworker when the decision was made.
relevance.FAIL-02: The source of the probable-cause timing rule that Hernandez draws on and that governs section 1983 removal claims in this circuit.

cases.case_name: Smith v. Organization of Foster Families for Equality & Reform
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court reversed, holding that even assuming foster families possess a protected liberty interest, New York's pre-removal procedures satisfied due process, and declining to decide whether such an interest exists.
cases.quote: whatever liberty interest may be argued to exist in the foster family is significantly weaker in the case of removals preceding return to the natural parent

relevance.ACT-03: The Supreme Court's controlling treatment of the foster family's asserted constitutional interest in a continuing foster placement.
relevance.ACT-04: Holds the asserted foster-family interest is weakest where the child is being returned to the natural parent, the premise of the foster-parent holding in Dupuy v. Samuels.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court affirmed invalidation of a grandparent visitation order, holding that Washington's statute as applied violated the mother's due process right to direct her children's upbringing because the trial court gave no special weight to a fit parent's own determination.
cases.quote: That aspect of the case is important, for there is a presumption that fit parents act in the best interests of their children.

relevance.OUT-03: The federal constitutional baseline In re R.L.S. operates against: a fit parent's decision must receive special weight over a non-parent's competing custody or visitation claim.
relevance.ACT-04: Limits how far a court may prefer a relative's contact or custody over the choices of a parent whose fitness has not been questioned.

cases.holding: The court held that a minor shown by clear and convincing evidence to be mature has a common-law right to consent to or refuse medical treatment, subject to countervailing state interests, and remanded with directions to expunge the neglect finding entered against the minor's mother.
cases.quote: Because we find that a mature minor may exercise a common law right to consent to or refuse medical care, we decline to address the constitutional issue.

relevance.ACT-06: The controlling Illinois authority on a juvenile court appointing a guardian to consent to urgent medical treatment for a minor over the minor's and the parent's objection.
relevance.INP-07: The case reached the juvenile court through the hospital treating a seventeen-year-old leukemia patient who refused blood transfusions.
relevance.FAIL-01: The neglect finding against the mother was ordered expunged once the mature-minor doctrine was recognized.

cases.holding: The court reversed an order terminating the wardship and DCFS guardianship of a nineteen-year-old, holding the circuit court made none of the written findings section 2-31(2) requires and that closure was against the manifest weight of the evidence, and remanded to extend wardship toward age twenty-one.
cases.quote: Aaron's lack of cooperation and failure to avail himself of the services could not by itself provide a sufficient basis to terminate his guardianship.

relevance.OUT-04: The leading published Illinois decision on continuing wardship and DCFS guardianship past nineteen to age twenty-one under section 2-31 of the Juvenile Court Act.
relevance.OUT-05: An order closing a youth's case without the statutory written findings about independence and the youth's wishes is ineffective.
relevance.FAIL-01: Reverses a case-closure decision as against the manifest weight of the evidence where the record showed the youth could not yet live independently.

cases.holding: The court affirmed as modified an order vacating DCFS guardianship and terminating wardship of an eighteen-year-old, directing that the public guardian be given leave to petition for reinstatement of wardship and guardianship at any time before the youth's twenty-first birthday.
cases.quote: There was no evidence in the record to indicate that Shawn B. possessed the skills and autonomy to successfully undertake independent living.

relevance.OUT-04: Holds that a young person may not simply be discharged at eighteen without regard to readiness for independent living, and preserves reinstatement of wardship up to twenty-one.
relevance.ACT-03: Measures the adequacy of the agency's succession of placements and programs by whether they actually prepared the ward to live on his own.
relevance.OUT-05: Case closure at the age of majority is not the end of the matter where reinstatement of wardship may still be sought.

cases.holding: The court upheld the constitutionality of the minor-requiring-authoritative-intervention statute and affirmed the adjudication as supported by a preponderance of the evidence, but reversed the dispositional order because the father was not given the notice the Act requires, and remanded.
cases.quote: The welfare of the minor is in jeopardy as a consequence of the minor's own behavior, not that of the parents.

relevance.INP-05: The Illinois pathway that opens when a youth or family seeks help: jurisdiction attaches only after interim crisis services are offered and the minor and parent cannot agree on a voluntary placement.
relevance.DEC-06: Illustrates the non-neglect, services-first track the Juvenile Court Act provides where the problem is the minor's own conduct rather than parental fault.

notes: Every case listed was retrieved from the CourtListener v4 API in this session (96 API calls total) and its opinion text read; no case or quotation is drawn from memory. Quotes are exact substrings of the retrieved opinion text with whitespace normalized, taken from the majority/lead opinion only. Where a CourtListener text carried OCR artifacts (PDF line-break hyphens such as 'pro- tective', or spaced en-dashes in statute numbers such as '2 — 28(3)'), a different sentence from the same opinion was selected so that no quote depends on a transcription artifact.

CourtListener captions many Illinois juvenile cases as 'People v. <parent's first name>'. Case names here use the style the Illinois courts use (In re Arthur H., In re D.T., In re D.C., In re J.J., In re Austin W., In re R.L.S., In re A.W., In re Curtis B., In re A.Z.), verified against the cluster's case_name_full field. The CourtListener URLs retain the platform's own slugs.

Date anomalies carried through from the CourtListener clusters, flagged for the reader: In re N.G. bears the public-domain citation 2018 IL 121939 but the cluster date_filed is 2019-02-05 (the opinion as modified upon denial of rehearing). Lassiter v. Department of Social Services shows 1981-08-28 (rehearing denied) rather than the June 1, 1981 decision date. B.H. v. McDonald shows 1995-04-07 (rehearing and rehearing en banc denied) rather than the February 23, 1995 decision date. In re S.L. shows 2014-03-03 although the opinion itself is captioned 'Filed January 24, 2014'.

Burris v. Department of Children & Family Services is given in N.E.2d slip form ('951 N.E.2d 1202 (Ill. App. Ct. 2011)') because the CourtListener cluster carries only the N.E.2d and Ill. Dec. parallel citations and no Ill. App. 3d citation; the official Illinois Appellate Reports citation was not retrieved in this session and is therefore not asserted.

OUT-04 (Extended Foster Care / Aging Out) is the weakest node. Targeted searches of ill and illappct for continued wardship past 18, youth in care over the age of majority, and reinstatement of wardship returned no published Illinois opinion construing 705 ILCS 405/2-31 wardship to age 21 or the state's extended foster care program. The two cases mapped (Brokaw v. Mercer County, where the plaintiff sued after reaching eighteen, and K.H. ex rel. Murphy v. Morgan, on the state's continuing duty for as long as the child remains in its custody) bear on the node only obliquely. A practitioner should treat OUT-04 as governed by statute and DCFS rule rather than by the case law collected here.

PMC-03 (Citizen Review Panels) and PMC-06 (systemic AI/pattern analysis) have no Illinois or Seventh Circuit case law at all. CAPTA's citizen review panel requirement, 42 U.S.C. 5106a(c), has generated no reported Illinois decision. The two cases mapped to each node (B.H. v. McDonald and Dupuy v. Samuels) are the closest analogues because in Illinois the independent-review and systemic-pattern-analysis functions have in practice been performed by federal consent-decree monitoring and class litigation rather than by a statutory panel. These entries are structural analogues, not authority on the panel requirement itself.

ACT-06 (Emergency Medical/Psychological Care) also has thin direct authority. No published Illinois opinion was located squarely on emergency medical or psychological treatment of a ward over parental objection in the abuse/neglect context; the three cases mapped touch the issue only through facts (DCFS as guardian consenting to treatment in In re Austin W.; hospital presentation and Pediatric Resource Center records in In re A.P.; the hospital fracture examination in Hernandez). Searches for psychotropic-medication and guardian-consent cases returned adult disabled-person guardianship decisions (Bernstein, In re Estate of Austwick, Plank v. A.M.P.) that are off point for child welfare and were excluded.

FAIL-03 (Federal Compliance Failure) has no Illinois state authority. CFSR and Single Audit Act findings are not litigated in Illinois courts; the node is served by the federal structural cases (B.H. v. McDonald, Dupuy v. Samuels, Doyle v. Camelot Care Centers), which are the actual enforcement mechanism in this jurisdiction.

No unpublished memorandum decisions were used. Every entry is a published opinion (CourtListener precedential_status 'Published'), including the two most recent Illinois Appellate Court decisions, In re A.M., 2025 IL App (1st) 242325, and In re K.W., 2026 IL App (1st) 251913.

ICWA coverage in Illinois is genuinely thin at the supreme court level. In re Z.L., 2021 IL 126931, is the only Illinois Supreme Court decision located that reaches ICWA, and it does so only to require remand for proof of notice compliance. The substantive qualified-expert-witness and active-efforts requirements are covered only by the appellate court (In re A.M., 2025). Illinois enacted its own state ICWA in 2022 (325 ILCS 5/ and related provisions); no published decision construing the state act was located in this session.

The layers.case_law.key_cases titles already in the IL node files (In re Marriage of Tronsrue, In re Estate of Coffman, In re Marriage of Arjmand, Doe v. Burke Wise Morrissey & Kaveny, In re Craig H., In re Estate of McDonald, In re Kelan W.) are identical across all 42 files and are keyword-matched noise. They were treated as candidate names only. None survived: they are marriage-dissolution, decedents' estates, adult guardianship or legal-malpractice cases with no bearing on any child-protection decision point. The single exception considered was 'In re V.S.', which does correspond to a real Illinois Supreme Court case (2025 IL 129755); it was independently retrieved, read, and is included here on its actual holding (mootness of an appeal challenging only one of two independent adjudicatory findings).

Two cases in this set were decided in Wisconsin-origin appeals but are binding Seventh Circuit precedent for Illinois: Michael C. v. Gresbach (school-premises searches during a child-abuse investigation) and Xiong v. Wagner (equal protection and section 1985(3) in a removal case). Both were retained because no published Illinois state decision was located on the same points; Hernandez v. Foster and Brokaw v. Mercer County, which arise from Illinois DCFS conduct, carry the removal and protective-custody analysis.

Missing (for a later pass): In re N.B., 191 Ill. 2d 338, 730 N.E.2d 1086 (2000) (CourtListener caption 'People v. Ca. R.') — verified by citation lookup. This is the source the brief's own two lead quotes rest on: both In re Arthur H. and In re A.P. state the preponderance burden and the mandatory-dismissal rule by citing N.B. The brief quotes the echoes and omits the origin, so DEC-01, DEC-05 and OUT-05 all cite downstream authority for a rule N.B. announced.

Missing (for a later pass): In re D.S., 217 Ill. 2d 306, 840 N.E.2d 1216 (2005) (CL caption 'In Re DS') — verified by citation lookup. Supplies the manifest-weight standard of review for neglect adjudications that In re A.P. applies at ¶17 and that every adjudicatory node (DEC-05, OUT-05, FAIL-01) silently depends on.

Missing (for a later pass): In re M.H., 196 Ill. 2d 356, 751 N.E.2d 1134 (2001) (CL caption 'People v. V.D.') — verified by citation lookup. Relied on in both In re Arthur H. and In re D.T. for why the clear-and-convincing standard attaches at unfitness; it is the Illinois bridge between Santosky and the two-step structure the brief attributes solely to In re D.T. at OUT-02.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Enis, 121 Ill. 2d 124, 520 N.E.2d 362 (1988) (CL caption 'People v. Enis') — verified by citation lookup. The Illinois Supreme Court's own application of Santosky, and the precedent In re D.T. expressly follows in choosing remand for a new hearing over independent appellate review of the evidence. Essential to OUT-02 and to any argument about the remedy for a wrong standard of proof.

Missing (for a later pass): In re C.N., 196 Ill. 2d 181, 752 N.E.2d 1030 (2001) (CL caption 'People v. Diane N.') — verified by citation lookup. The leading Illinois Supreme Court decision on whether and how compliance with a DCFS service plan figures in the section 1(D)(m) reasonable-progress ground. ACT-02 currently rests on In re S.L. and In re D.C., which address the pleading of the nine-month period and which children it reaches, but never the substantive content of reasonable progress.

Missing (for a later pass): In re D.W., 214 Ill. 2d 289, 827 N.E.2d 466 (2005) (CL caption 'People v. Lisa M.') — verified by citation lookup. The controlling Illinois authority on the depravity ground and its rebuttable presumption; In re N.G. reasons directly from it. OUT-02 cites N.G. for the limit on the conviction route without the case that supplies the framework N.G. is limiting.

Missing (for a later pass): In re D.F., 208 Ill. 2d 223, 802 N.E.2d 800 (2003) (CL caption 'People v. Lashawn F.') — verified by citation lookup. The Illinois Supreme Court's reasonable-efforts and expedition decision, cited in In re D.T. ACT-02 and OUT-01 discuss court-ordered services and reunification with no Illinois authority on the reasonable-efforts findings that IV-E funding turns on.

Missing (for a later pass): Iseberg v. Gross, 227 Ill. 2d 78, 879 N.E.2d 278 (2007) — verified by citation lookup. The special-relationship/affirmative-duty case Doe-3 applies at ¶24-25. Since INP-01 and INP-02 are left with Doe-3 alone after the drops above, the authority Doe-3 itself rests on should be in the brief.

Missing (for a later pass): Doe v. Heck, 327 F.3d 492 (7th Cir. 2003) — cited as controlling in the retrieved Gresbach opinion ('Heck, 327 F.3d at 512'). The foundational Seventh Circuit decision on child-abuse investigations conducted at private schools and on parents' and children's Fourth Amendment and familial-relations rights during CPS interviews. INP-08 and DEC-02 currently cite Gresbach, which merely applies Heck.

Missing (for a later pass): Siliven v. Indiana Department of Child Services, 635 F.3d 921 (7th Cir. 2011) — cited as controlling in the retrieved Hernandez opinion ('siliven, 635 F.3d at 927'), and it is the case Hernandez draws its probable-cause timing rule from. DEC-04, INP-12 and FAIL-02 quote Hernandez for a proposition Siliven supplies.

Missing (for a later pass): Smith v. Organization of Foster Families for Equality & Reform, 431 U.S. 816 (1977) — quoted in the retrieved Dupuy opinion. The Supreme Court's controlling treatment of the foster family's asserted liberty interest, which is the premise of Dupuy's foster-parent holding and directly relevant to ACT-03 and ACT-04.

Missing (for a later pass): Troxel v. Granville, 530 U.S. 57 (2000) — the constitutional baseline for a fit parent's right to direct upbringing against a non-parent's custody or visitation claim. OUT-03 rests entirely on In re R.L.S. for when a non-parent may take guardianship over a fit parent's objection; the federal rule R.L.S. operates against is absent from the brief.

GAP-CLOSING PASS (this session): all twelve authorities the verifier flagged as missing were searched for by name and citation on CourtListener, retrieved as clusters and opinions, read in full, and added below. None failed verification; there is no unverifiable authority to report. The 'Missing (for a later pass)' notes above are retained as the provenance record of why each was sought, but they are now superseded — each of those cases is in the cases array.

Added In re N.B., 191 Ill. 2d 338, 730 N.E.2d 1086 (2000), for DEC-01, DEC-05 and OUT-05: it is the Illinois Supreme Court's own statement of the preponderance burden (with its definition, 'proof that makes the condition more probable than not') and of the mandatory-dismissal consequence that In re Arthur H. and In re A.P. merely echo, and it ordered the neglect petitions dismissed on the facts.

Added In re D.S., 217 Ill. 2d 306, 840 N.E.2d 1216 (2005), for DEC-05, OUT-05, FAIL-01 and INP-07: it supplies the manifest-weight standard of review that every adjudicatory node silently depends on, and it also settles that a wardship petition may be sustained in Illinois for a child delivered out of state. Cluster date_filed is 2005-12-01.

Added In re M.H., 196 Ill. 2d 356, 751 N.E.2d 1134 (2001), for OUT-02 and FAIL-01: it is the Illinois bridge between Santosky and the two-step termination structure, and it holds that due process requires a factual-basis determination before a circuit court may accept a parent's admission of unfitness.

Added In re Enis, 121 Ill. 2d 124, 520 N.E.2d 362 (1988), for OUT-02 and FAIL-01: the Illinois Supreme Court's own application of Santosky, invalidating section 1(D)(f) of the Adoption Act and fixing the remedy for a wrong standard of proof as a new hearing rather than appellate reweighing. CourtListener captions the cluster 'People v. Enis'; case_name_full is 'In re Sabrina Enis'. The cluster's combined text also carries a special concurrence joined by Justice Miller; the quote used is from Justice Ward's majority opinion.

Added In re C.N., 196 Ill. 2d 181, 752 N.E.2d 1030 (2001), for ACT-02, ACT-01 and OUT-02: the leading Illinois decision on the substantive content of the section 1(D)(m) reasonable-progress ground, holding the benchmark takes in service-plan compliance and court directives measured against both the removal conditions and conditions later discovered. This is the authority ACT-02 previously lacked.

Added In re D.W., 214 Ill. 2d 289, 827 N.E.2d 466 (2005), for OUT-02 and FAIL-05: it supplies the conviction-based unfitness framework, and the contrast between section 1(D)(i)'s rebuttable depravity presumption and section 1(D)(q)'s irrebuttable one, that In re N.G. later operates on.

Added In re D.F., 208 Ill. 2d 223, 802 N.E.2d 800 (2003), for ACT-02, OUT-01 and OUT-02: it holds the nine-month evaluation period applies to the reasonable-efforts ground as well as reasonable progress and runs from adjudication, and states the Juvenile Court Act's expedition-and-permanency policy. The quote is the majority's statement of statutory purpose; the opinion's formal holding sentence exceeds the 30-word quote limit and so was placed in the holding field instead.

Added Iseberg v. Gross, 227 Ill. 2d 78, 879 N.E.2d 278 (2007), for INP-01 and INP-02: the affirmative-duty and special-relationship framework Doe-3 applies, which is why an Illinois reporting obligation must be statutory under ANCRA rather than common law. The retrieved text carries spaced-en-dash OCR artifacts in statute numbers ('2 — 615'); the quote avoids them.

Added Doe v. Heck, 327 F.3d 492 (7th Cir. 2003), for INP-08, DEC-02 and FAIL-02: the foundational circuit decision on child-abuse investigations at private schools, which Michael C. v. Gresbach applies. The court held the warrantless school search and seizure unconstitutional while granting qualified immunity because the right was not then clearly established; the holding field states both halves.

Added Siliven v. Indiana Department of Child Services, 635 F.3d 921 (7th Cir. 2011), for DEC-04, INP-12 and FAIL-02: the source of the probable-cause framework Hernandez v. Foster draws on. Siliven is an Indiana-origin appeal but is binding Seventh Circuit precedent for Illinois, on the same footing as Michael C. v. Gresbach and Xiong v. Wagner. The retrieved text is a PDF conversion with line-break hyphens ('con- sidered', 'case- workers'); the quote was chosen from a clean sentence.

Added Smith v. Organization of Foster Families for Equality & Reform, 431 U.S. 816 (1977), for ACT-03 and ACT-04: the Supreme Court's controlling treatment of the foster family's asserted liberty interest, which is the premise of the foster-parent holding in Dupuy v. Samuels. The quote is from Justice Brennan's opinion for the Court, not from the concurrences in the same cluster.

Added Troxel v. Granville, 530 U.S. 57 (2000), for OUT-03 and ACT-04: the federal constitutional baseline against which In re R.L.S. operates. The quote is from Justice O'Connor's plurality opinion, which is the lead opinion; the cluster also contains concurrences and dissents that were not quoted.

ACT-06 gap closed: added In re E.G., 133 Ill. 2d 98, 549 N.E.2d 322 (1989), for ACT-06, INP-07 and FAIL-01. This supersedes the earlier note that no published Illinois opinion was found on medical treatment of a minor over objection in a child-protection posture. E.G. arose under the Juvenile Court Act — the circuit court appointed a guardian to consent to blood transfusions for a seventeen-year-old leukemia patient and entered a neglect finding against her mother — and the Illinois Supreme Court recognized the mature-minor doctrine and ordered the neglect finding expunged. ACT-06 now has two cases (In re Austin W. and In re E.G.); it remains a thin node, and emergency treatment of a younger child over parental objection is still governed by statute and DCFS rule rather than by any decision located here.

OUT-04 gap closed: added In re Aaron L., 2013 IL App (1st) 122808, 988 N.E.2d 688, and In re Shawn B., 218 Ill. App. 3d 374, 578 N.E.2d 269 (1991), for OUT-04 (and OUT-05, FAIL-01, ACT-03). This supersedes the earlier note that no published Illinois opinion construes 705 ILCS 405/2-31 wardship to age 21. Aaron L. is directly on section 2-31(2): it reverses a case closure entered without the required written findings about the youth's wishes and capacity for independent living, and holds that a youth's lack of cooperation with services cannot by itself justify closure. Shawn B. preserves the right to petition for reinstatement of wardship and DCFS guardianship any time before the twenty-first birthday. Both are Appellate Court decisions; no Illinois Supreme Court decision on extended foster care or aging out was located, and the statutory and DCFS-rule caveat in the earlier note still applies.

INP-05 gap closed: added In re J.M., 170 Ill. App. 3d 552, 524 N.E.2d 1241 (1988), for INP-05 and DEC-06. The minor-requiring-authoritative-intervention track under the Juvenile Court Act is Illinois' statutory front door for a youth or family seeking help without a maltreatment allegation: jurisdiction attaches only after the minor has been taken into limited custody, offered interim crisis intervention services, and the minor and parent have failed to agree on a voluntary alternative placement. J.M. also upholds the statute against constitutional attack and reverses the disposition for defective notice to the father. No Illinois Supreme Court decision on voluntary or FFPSA-style prevention services was located.

Node_map convention: as in the reconciled brief, node_map is a curated selection rather than a mechanical inversion of every relevance key. It was rebuilt this pass so that (a) every one of the 42 nodes carries between two and six cases, (b) mappings already asserted in existing cases' relevance objects but omitted from the old node_map (for example Dupuy v. Samuels at INP-02 and Doyle v. Camelot at PMC-01) are now reflected, and (c) no case in the array is unmapped. Three nodes attracted more than six candidates — FAIL-01 (14), OUT-02 (12) and OUT-05 (10) — and were trimmed to the six most on-point; the cases trimmed out of those lists all remain mapped at another node, and their relevance objects still record the connection for a reader working from a case rather than from a node.

Case count: this jurisdiction now carries 53 distinct cases, above the 20-40 target. The overage is deliberate. Sixteen cases were added under explicit instruction — twelve named by the verifier as leading authorities the brief was citing around, and four (In re E.G., In re Aaron L., In re Shawn B., In re J.M.) to close the ACT-06, OUT-04 and INP-05 coverage gaps. No existing entry was removed, since removals were outside the scope of this pass. A future pass could prune the most redundant entries at OUT-02 and FAIL-01.

This pass used roughly 40 additional CourtListener v4 API calls (searches, cluster lookups and opinion retrievals), all paced at one request every two seconds. Every one of the sixteen added cases was retrieved as a cluster and its opinion text read in this session; each quote was then machine-verified as an exact substring of that retrieved text after whitespace and curly-quote normalization. Two candidate quotes were rejected and replaced during that check because the CourtListener text broke the sentence with a PDF line-break hyphen (Siliven) or exceeded the thirty-word limit (In re D.F., In re Enis, Doe v. Heck).

Missing (for a later pass): In re Adoption of Syck, 138 Ill. 2d 255, 562 N.E.2d 174 (1990) — confirmed by citation in the retrieved In re M.H. text ('Syck, 138 Ill.2d at 275'). The foundational Illinois Supreme Court decision on the two-step termination structure, the clear-and-convincing unfitness burden, and manifest-weight review of an unfitness finding. OUT-02 runs Santosky to Enis to M.H. to D.T. and skips the case each of them cites for the unfitness standard and its standard of review.

Missing (for a later pass): In re D.L., 191 Ill. 2d 1, 727 N.E.2d 990 (2000) — confirmed by citation in the retrieved In re D.F. text ('See In re D.L., 191 Ill.2d 1, 10'). The Illinois Supreme Court decision D.F. relies on for the proposition that the statutory evaluation period applies to both the reasonable-efforts and the reasonable-progress grounds of section 1(D)(m). ACT-02 quotes D.F. for a rule D.L. supplies.

Missing (for a later pass): Lulay v. Lulay, 193 Ill. 2d 455, 739 N.E.2d 521 (2000) — confirmed by citation in the retrieved In re M.H. text ('Lulay, 193 Ill.2d at 470-71'). The Illinois Supreme Court's own application of Troxel, protecting a fit parent's decision about a non-parent's contact with the child. OUT-03 and ACT-04 pair In re R.L.S. with Troxel and omit the Illinois decision that domesticates Troxel.

Missing (for a later pass): Julie Q. v. Department of Children & Family Services, 2013 IL 113783 — verified on CourtListener (cluster 1086761, Illinois Supreme Court, 2013-10-23). The leading recent Illinois Supreme Court decision on the validity of an indicated finding, holding DCFS lacked statutory authority under ANCRA to indicate a report on an 'environment injurious' theory. Absent from DEC-01, DEC-03 and FAIL-01, which rest on Lyon, Dupuy, Doyle and Burris.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Gwynne P., 215 Ill. 2d 340, 830 N.E.2d 508 (2005) — verified on CourtListener (cluster 2059071, Illinois Supreme Court, 2005-05-19). Illinois Supreme Court authority on the reasonable-progress ground and what evidence a court may consider in assessing a parent's progress within the statutory period. ACT-02 has C.N., D.F., S.L. and D.C. but not Gwynne P.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Christopher K., 217 Ill. 2d 348, 841 N.E.2d 945 (2005) — verified on CourtListener (clusters 2132782 and 3135187, Illinois Supreme Court, 2005-12-15). The Illinois Supreme Court's principal decision on conflict of interest and effective assistance of counsel in termination proceedings, and the direct predecessor In re Br. M. builds on. OUT-02 and FAIL-01 cite Br. M. for the closed set of per se conflicts without the case that established the framework.

Missing (for a later pass): Nichol v. Stass, 192 Ill. 2d 233, 735 N.E.2d 582 (2000) — verified on CourtListener (cluster 2094760, Illinois Supreme Court, 2000-08-10). The leading Illinois decision on foster-parent immunity arising from the death of a child in a foster home. FAIL-04 and OUT-06 rest entirely on federal law (DeShaney, K.H.) plus a discovery ruling (Harris) and have no Illinois state authority on liability for a child's death in care.

Missing (for a later pass): Wallace v. Smyth, 203 Ill. 2d 441, 786 N.E.2d 980 (2002) — verified on CourtListener (Illinois Supreme Court, 2002-12-19). Illinois Supreme Court authority on the duty owed to a child who died in a residential child care facility and the scope of in loco parentis immunity. Directly relevant to OUT-06 and FAIL-04, where residential and congregate-care fatalities are unaddressed.

Missing (for a later pass): In re M.M., 156 Ill. 2d 53, 619 N.E.2d 702 (1993) (CourtListener caption 'Morgan v. Parents of M.M.', cluster 7079904) — verified by citation lookup. The leading Illinois Supreme Court decision on the division of authority between the juvenile court and DCFS as guardian, including the court's power to impose conditions on the guardian's consent to adoption. ACT-03 addresses that division through In re Austin W. alone; M.M. is the case Austin W. builds on.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Lawrence M., 172 Ill. 2d 523, 670 N.E.2d 710 (1996) — verified on CourtListener (cluster 2015227, Illinois Supreme Court, 1996-08-02). Illinois Supreme Court authority on standing and party status in juvenile court proceedings, including siblings' interests. Nothing in the brief addresses who may participate in an Illinois abuse and neglect proceeding, a gap touching DEC-05 and INP-04.
